lead: This unit turns a problem on paper into a running Python program. You learn to plan with algorithms and flowcharts, then write, run and correct small programs using variables, data types, operators, input and output. After it you can read a simple Python file, predict what it prints, and fix the common errors it throws.
about: Unit 1 builds the base for the whole course. Chapter 1.1 shows how to turn a word problem into an algorithm, a flowchart and pseudocode before any code exists. Chapter 1.2 explains why Python exists and gets your first program to run; 1.3 shows the two ways to run it, typing at the >>> prompt or running a saved file. Chapter 1.4 sets the naming rules and 1.5 gives the data types those names can hold. Chapter 1.6 combines values with operators and fixes the order of evaluation. Chapter 1.7 adds input, printing, comments and indentation, which Python uses for blocks instead of braces. Chapter 1.8 teaches you to read an error message and find the bug. Control flow, functions, lists and dictionaries come in later units.

chapters.idea: A program is written twice, first as a plan in plain steps and only then as code.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this subtopic, so keep it short. Cover what an algorithm is: a finite, ordered set of unambiguous steps with a clear stop. Name the three control constructs: sequence, selection, repetition. Give the standard flowchart symbols: oval for start/stop, parallelogram for input/output, rectangle for a process, diamond for a decision. Pseudocode is plain English with IF ... THEN ... ELSE and WHILE ... ENDWHILE. Some syllabi call the written plan a problem analysis chart, with boxes for inputs, required outputs, processing and alternative solutions. Do not write Python syntax in this chapter.

figure.title: Plan for the shop bill
figure.aria: A flowchart that starts, reads the number of pens and notebooks, computes the bill at ₹12 and ₹45, prints it and stops.

chapters.example: A shop sells a pen for ₹12 and a notebook for ₹45. Draw a flowchart and write pseudocode that reads the number of pens and notebooks bought and prints the bill. Test the plan with 3 pens and 2 notebooks: bill = 3 × 12 + 2 × 45 = 36 + 90 = ₹126.
chapters.trap: Decisions belong in a diamond and processes in a rectangle. A decision drawn in a rectangle loses the branching, and the marks with it.
chapters.leave: All Python syntax, loops and functions go to Unit 2; only the planning of the solution belongs here.

chapters.idea: Python trades speed for readability, so a short, clear program does real work with no boilerplate.
chapters.depth: Why Python: readable syntax, free and open source, runs on Windows, Linux and macOS, a large standard library, used in web work, data work and automation. History: created by Guido van Rossum, first public release in 1991, named after the comedy group Monty Python; Python 3 arrived in 2008; Python 2 support ended in January 2020, so write Python 3. Features: interpreted, dynamically typed, indentation-based blocks, automatic memory management. First program: one statement print("Hello, India"). No header, no semicolon, no main function. Show exactly what the screen shows. Say that a program is saved as name.py and run, with details left to 1.3 and 1.8.

figure.aria: A timeline showing Python 2 releases from 2000, Python 2.7 ending in 2020, and Python 3 running from 2008 to today.

chapters.example: Type this two-line program, save it as hello.py and run it: print("Hello, India") then print("-" * 10). The screen shows Hello, India on the first line and exactly 10 dashes on the second line.
chapters.trap: The >>> prompt is not part of the code. Typing it inside a saved file gives a SyntaxError on the first line.
chapters.prereq: 1.1 for the idea of a step-by-step plan.
chapters.leave: The two running modes in detail go to 1.3, error types to 1.8, and modules and packages to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: The same Python code can be typed a line at a time or saved and run as a file, and the difference is what survives.
chapters.depth: Interactive mode: the >>> prompt, also called the REPL (read, evaluate, print, loop). Type 12 * 8 and 96 appears at once. Values vanish when you exit. Good for testing one line. Script mode: write lines in a file, save as area.py, run python area.py; the file runs top to bottom and the names stay alive only while it runs. Show the same calculation both ways. Mention IDLE as one editor among many, in a line. Debugging means fixing what the interpreter reports; full detail is in 1.8.

figure.aria: Two sessions: the typed expression 12 * 8 answers 96 at the prompt, and the saved file area.py also prints 96.

chapters.example: Compute 12 × 8 both ways. Interactive: type 12 * 8 at the >>> prompt and get 96; exiting throws the result away. Script: put print(12 * 8) in a file area.py and run python area.py, which prints 96 again. Same answer, but the file keeps the steps for tomorrow.
chapters.trap: Believing names typed in interactive mode still exist next time. A new session starts empty; only a saved script repeats the same steps.
chapters.prereq: 1.2 for a first program to run.
chapters.leave: Tracebacks and error families go to 1.8; opening and closing files goes to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: A variable is a name stuck onto a value, and the name must follow fixed rules.
chapters.depth: A variable is created by assignment; there is no type declaration. Dynamic typing: one name can hold an int now and a string later. Rules for identifiers: letters a–z and A–Z, digits and underscore; cannot start with a digit; case sensitive, so Total and total differ; no keyword; no spaces or hyphens. List the common keywords: False, None, True, and, as, assert, break, class, continue, def, del, elif, else, except, finally, for, from, global, if, import, in, is, lambda, not, or, pass, raise, return, try, while, with, yield. Say the exact set changes with the version and help('keywords') prints it. Show multiple assignment x = y = 5, the swap a, b = b, a, and del. Suggest snake_case for ordinary names.

figure.title: Names after three assignments
figure.aria: Three names, price, qty and bill, holding 45, 3 and the computed value 135.

chapters.example: Which of these are valid identifiers: total_marks, 2nd_rank, _temp, my-var, class, Price? Valid: total_marks, _temp, Price. Invalid: 2nd_rank (starts with a digit), my-var (hyphen), class (a keyword). Then run price = 45, qty = 3, bill = price * qty, and bill holds 135.
chapters.trap: A name has no value before its first assignment. Printing it then raises NameError; it does not quietly hold 0.
chapters.prereq: 1.3, script mode, where names live while the file runs.
chapters.leave: What each name may hold goes to 1.5; scope and lifetime go to Unit 2; mutability and object identity go to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: Every value has a type, the type decides what the value can do, and conversion changes the type on purpose.
chapters.depth: Numbers: int (whole, unlimited size, so 2 ** 100 is fine), float (binary floating point, so 0.1 + 0.2 gives 0.30000000000000004), complex (3 + 4j). str: text in single or double quotes, immutable, with a preview of indexing only. bool: True and False, and True + True gives 2 because bool counts as a kind of int. type(x) reports the type. Conversion: int(), float(), str(), bool(); implicit promotion when an int meets a float. int("42") works, int("4.5") raises ValueError, bool(0) is False but bool("0") is True. Some syllabi call explicit conversion casting. Lists, tuples, dictionaries and sets belong to Unit 3 in one line only.

figure.aria: A tree of Python value types: value splits into number, str and bool, and number splits into int, float and complex.

chapters.trap: input() always gives a string, and int("4.5") is a ValueError. Convert to float first, then to int if you really need a whole number.
chapters.prereq: 1.4, because a name must exist before it can hold a typed value.
chapters.leave: Lists, tuples, dictionaries and sets go to Unit 3; user-defined classes go to Unit 4; string methods go to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: An expression is evaluated by precedence first and left-to-right order second.
chapters.depth: Operands, operators, expressions. Arithmetic: + − * / (true division, always a float) // (floor division) % (remainder) ** (power, right associative). Precedence high to low: **, unary −, then * / // %, then + −, then comparisons < > <= >= == !=, then not, then and, then or. Same level goes left to right, except ** and unary minus, so -2 ** 2 is -4. Mixed int and float gives a float. Augmented assignment += -= *=. Comparisons and logical operators return True or False, while and/or hand back one of the operands. Built-in functions inside expressions: abs(), round(), int(), len(). One line on import math and math.sqrt(16); modules and packages are Unit 5.

figure.aria: The parse tree of 2 + 3 * 4 ** 2 - 10 // 3, with minus at the root and the power operator deepest in the tree.

chapters.trap: / always gives a float and // rounds down, not toward zero: -7 // 2 is -4 and -7 % 2 is 1, not -1.
chapters.prereq: 1.5, since the types of the two operands decide the type of the result.
chapters.leave: if and loop statements go to Unit 2; operator overloading goes to Unit 4; the full math library goes to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Python reads text from the keyboard as a string, and it reads structure from indentation.
chapters.depth: print() writes to the screen; print(a, b, sep=', ', end='\n'), where sep sits between items and end comes after the last one. input() always returns a string, so numbers need int(input()) or float(input()); input("Enter marks: ") shows the prompt first. Comments start with # and run to the end of the line; a triple-quoted string can serve as a note or docstring. Indentation marks a block: a header ending in a colon needs an indented line under it, statements with the same indent belong together, four spaces is the convention, and tabs must never be mixed with spaces. Blank lines are ignored. A backslash or an open bracket continues a long line.

figure.title: One prompt and one greeting
figure.aria: A chain from the input prompt, to the name variable holding Ravi, to print, to the greeting Hello Ravi on screen.

chapters.example: Ask for a name and a birth year, then print "Ravi, you are 24 years old in 2025". Inputs: Ravi and 2001. Code: name = input("Name: "), year = int(input("Birth year: ")), print(name + ", you are", 2025 - year, "years old in 2025"). The subtraction gives 2025 - 2001 = 24.
chapters.trap: Forgetting int() around input(). Then 2025 - "2001" raises TypeError, and "Total:" + 5 raises TypeError too, while print("Total:", 5) is fine.
chapters.prereq: 1.6 for the expressions you put inside print() and around input().
chapters.leave: if and while bodies go to Unit 2; reading from files goes to Unit 5; f-string formatting detail goes to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: Three error families look different, and the traceback tells you which one you have.
chapters.depth: SyntaxError: Python cannot parse the line and nothing runs — missing colon, unbalanced bracket, misspelled keyword. IndentationError and TabError are syntax-error subclasses. Runtime error: the line is valid but fails while running — ZeroDivisionError, NameError (name not defined, often a typo), TypeError (int + str), ValueError (int("abc")). Semantic error: the program runs to the end and prints the wrong thing, with no message at all. How to debug: read a traceback from the bottom line up, note the file and line number, then reproduce with the smallest input and print intermediate values. Do not teach try and except here; that is Unit 5.

figure.title: Which error, when
figure.aria: A decision flow: the file is read whole, bad syntax stops it at once, a crash stops it mid-run, and a wrong result runs to the end with no message.

chapters.example: The task is the average of 10 and 20, which is 15. Classify four attempts: (a) print(10 + 20 / 2) prints 20.0, a semantic error; (b) print(10 / 2 + missing) raises NameError while running, a runtime error; (c) print(10 + 20 / 2 with the closing bracket missing is a SyntaxError and nothing runs; (d) print(10 / 0) raises ZeroDivisionError while running.
chapters.trap: A misspelled function name such as prnt() is a NameError at runtime, not a syntax error. Syntax errors are grammar only, like a missing colon or bracket.
chapters.prereq: 1.2 to 1.7, because you need working code before you can break it.
chapters.leave: try, except, else and finally go to Unit 5; a full debugger tool is not part of this syllabus.

links: the flowchart and pseudocode become the lines you type
the first program runs at the prompt or from a saved file
a saved script holds its values in named variables
every name holds a value of some data type
the data type decides which operators work and what they return

bad indentation or input shows up as an error to debug
a wrong type conversion appears as a runtime error
the algorithm tells you the right answer, so the bug shows
